children: Jaundice is a symptom, not a disease, and identifying its underlying cause is key to timely treatment and avoiding unnecessary dietary restrictions

It is not uncommon to meet patients who diagnose themselves even before they step into my office. One condition that brings out the medical practitioner in all of us is jaundice. Once there is the slightest sign of yellowness in the eyes, home treatment begins; their diets become limited, and eventually, all sweet food items vanish. People generally realise they are suffering from jaundice when a relative tells them that their eyes look yellow, or when they look in the mirror and find yellow patches in the sclera (the whites of the eyes).

However, jaundice may also be a first sign of some trouble within the liver, the gallbladder, or the blood. The truth is that the yellow coloration itself is a symptom. Jaundice results from the accumulation of bilirubin, which is a substance produced during the breakdown of old red blood cells. However, this symptom does not explain the reason for it, which is where patients and some doctors who are still new in their profession commit the error of considering jaundice to be one specific condition. This is not the case because jaundice is actually a symptom that is common to various unrelated diseases, and it all depends on the cause.

The process of bilirubin circulation is usually well structured. It appears during the natural destruction of old red blood cells, further passes through liver processing, and moves via the gallbladder and bile ducts to the intestine, after which it is excreted from the body. Jaundice occurs when something interferes with this cycle, and there are three stages of such interference.

First, there can be too much bilirubin production before it even reaches the liver in cases of certain genetic problems related to blood or rapid destruction of red blood cells. Another reason for jaundice can be the dysfunction of the liver, for example, in cases of viral hepatitis, alcoholic injury, fatty liver disease, side effects of medications, or autoimmune disorders.

In the third group of diseases, the liver processes the bilirubin normally, but for some reasons cannot excrete it. It can occur due to such reasons as gallstones, bile ducts stenosis, and rarely tumours in the pancreas or bile ducts that create an obstruction and lead to the accumulation of bilirubin in the blood vessels. Although all the symptoms of this disease are similar, the differences in the mechanism are significant.

Moreover, all types of jaundice do not mean a severe form of liver ailment. Gilbert’s syndrome, which is a benign and relatively frequent genetic problem in India, is a situation where the skin turns yellow, and this happens in a mild and sporadic manner, usually when one fasts or gets sick or stressed; there is no liver injury in this condition. This does not require any specific treatment other than establishing the fact that it is really Gilbert’s syndrome. In addition, jaundice in babies is very frequent and usually transient, resulting from an adjustment of their liver to handling bilirubin independently in the early days of life.

This is also important from a wellbeing perspective because jaundice can often lead people to make sudden changes to their everyday habits without knowing what their body actually needs. Food restrictions, avoiding certain activities, or constantly monitoring the colour of the eyes can become part of daily life when people are unsure about the underlying cause.

Once the cause has been identified, patients can approach their diet, routine and recovery with greater clarity and continue with their everyday lives in a more balanced manner. The aim should be to give the body the appropriate care while also allowing the person to maintain their energy, independence and quality of life. Understanding the cause of jaundice therefore helps not only in choosing the right treatment, but also in helping patients make sensible choices about their everyday wellbeing.

However, some instances of jaundice need to be evaluated immediately by the medical profession rather than following the watch-and-wait principle. Presence of jaundice along with fever and pain in the abdomen is indicative of infection in an obstructed bile duct, also known as cholangitis. In addition, presence of confusion, sleepiness, or bruising along with jaundice is indicative of acute liver failure where the functions of the liver are affected and may need ICU care with a few patients requiring urgent liver transplantation.

Unexplained development of painless jaundice slowly in a patient in his/her senior years could be due to a tumour obstructing the bile duct and thus requires immediate imaging. The association of other symptoms with the onset of jaundice is what matters rather than the degree of jaundice. Think of the yellowness as a gentle warning light rather than a definitive diagnosis. Your path forward depends entirely on how quickly you choose to respect that warning and seek real care.
Guest Author Dr. Piramanayagam P | MBBS, MD (General Medicine) | DM (Gastroenterology) | Senior Consultant | Gastroenterology and Hepatology | Apollo Hospitals |
